concerns: Assay sensitivity and material yield — particle-peak immuno-capture fractions often contain low biomass; targeted miRNA and proteomics assays may lack sensitivity without prior analytical validation and adequate input material.

False-positive risk from co‑isolates — tightly bound soluble complexes or lipoproteins that co-fractionate can mimic membrane-protected signals unless orthogonal controls (detergent/protease + spike-in tracers + negative capture controls) are rigorously applied, per MISEV2023.

Process sensitivity and scale-up — capture reagent performance, fractionation yield, and particle:protein ratios can change substantially during TFF/SEC or scale-up; without demonstrating consistent recovery and panel detectability on scaled lots, the fingerprint cannot serve as a comparability gate.

Stability and storage — no stability data provided for protected RNAs/proteins in capture-positive fractions after storage or common process hold steps; degradation could cause apparent lot-to-lot variability unrelated to manufacturing.

Lot comparability vs potency relevance — even if reproducible across lots, the fingerprint is exploratory and not evidence of delivery or functional potency; nonhuman-primate biodistribution (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution) highlights uncertainty about translation of rodent-derived cargo relevance to larger species.

Measurement feasibility — targeted proteomics (SRM/PRM) and targeted small-RNA assays require defined standards and careful spike-in normalization; the proposal assumes these are pre-validated but they must be demonstrated on intended fraction matrices before use for gating.
conclusion: Supported as an exploratory, early-stage manufacturing/comparability characterization strategy but not yet sufficient as an operational lot gate or potency surrogate. The proposed small, protected-cargo panel approach aligns with MISEV2023 recommendations for orthogonal, membrane-protection controls and addresses source-cell consistency considerations from rodent studies, and it is manufacturable at scale in principle. Critical gaps remain (assay sensitivity in low-biomass, risk of co‑isolated soluble complexes producing false-positive “protected” signals, demonstrable recovery and reproducibility across scaled lots, and relevance to in vivo delivery in larger species). Before this can be used for lot gating or regulatory comparability decisions the program must (1) analytically validate capture reagents and sensitivity on the expected particle-peak yields; (2) demonstrate robust spike-in recovery and detergent/protease discrimination across ≥3 independent production lots including scaled-process lots and stability-timepoints; and (3) show that the fingerprint is not reproducibly produced by non‑EV co‑isolates (orthogonal negative controls). Until those validation milestones are met, treat the fingerprint as an exploratory lot-characterization attribute only.
evidence_gap: Key gaps: (1) large-animal/nonhuman-primate biodistribution casts doubt on intranasal delivery and therefore on the downstream relevance of an EV-protected cargo gate to in vivo delivery; (2) no evidence in provided sources that the proposed targeted-panel assays are sensitive and reproducible on low-biomass, immuno-captured particle-peak fractions or on scaled production lots; (3) stability/aging data for protected cargos in finished drug-substance and post-scale‑up process variability data are missing.
